fly-creation.title: Not Even a Fly
fly-creation.hook: No one has ever created a fly. Scientists have now mapped a fly's whole brain, and still cannot build one.
fly-creation.science.0: A housefly eats solid food by spitting digestive fluid onto it, letting it dissolve, and sucking it up. Fruit flies are among the best-studied animals on Earth: since Thomas Hunt Morgan's “fly room” of 1910 they have taught us how genes, chromosomes and development work.
fly-creation.science.1: In 2024 the FlyWire project published the complete wiring diagram of a fruit fly's brain: 139,255 neurons and more than 50 million connections between them. It is one of the great mapping feats of biology.
fly-creation.science.2: Yet nobody has built a fly, or even a living cell, from non-living parts. In 2010 Craig Venter's team made a bacterium run on a chemically synthesised genome, but they had to put that genome into an existing cell.

fly-creation.proof.1.title: Morgan's fly room
fly-creation.proof.1.text: Thomas Hunt Morgan finds a white-eyed fruit fly and shows that genes sit on chromosomes. Nobel Prize 1933. The fruit fly becomes the best-studied animal in genetics.
fly-creation.proof.2.title: The fly's genome
fly-creation.proof.2.text: The genome of the fruit fly is sequenced: about 14,000 genes.
fly-creation.proof.3.title: Venter: a synthetic genome
fly-creation.proof.3.text: Craig Venter's team makes a bacterium run on a chemically synthesised genome, but the genome has to be placed inside an existing living cell.

fly-creation.proof.4.text: The FlyWire project publishes the complete wiring diagram of a fruit fly's brain: 139,255 neurons and more than 50 million connections.

fly-creation.fit.0: A fly is among the smallest complete animals and no one has assembled one from parts; even its genome has about 14,000 genes working together.
fly-creation.fit.1: Science can now map and read a fly in exquisite detail and still cannot make life from non-life.
fly-creation.gap.0: Classical commentators read “if the fly snatches something from them” as flies eating the sweet offerings left before idols, which the idols could not recover. The digestion reading is modern.
fly-creation.gap.1: Synthetic biology rewrites genomes, so whether “create” is met depends on what counts as creating.
fly-creation.gap.2: The verse is an argument against idol worship, not a lesson in biology.

mosquito-example.title: The Mosquito and What Is Above It
mosquito-example.hook: God is not ashamed to use a mosquito as an example, and the smallest creature can be the deadliest.
mosquito-example.science.0: Female mosquitoes carry malaria, dengue, yellow fever and Zika. Malaria alone still kills about 600,000 people a year, most of them young children (WHO).
mosquito-example.science.1: That the mosquito is the carrier was found out between 1880 and 1900. In 1880 Alphonse Laveran saw the malaria parasite in human blood. In 1897 Ronald Ross found its developing stages in the gut of an Anopheles mosquito, work that won the 1902 Nobel Prize. In 1900 an American commission under Walter Reed confirmed that yellow fever is also spread by mosquitoes.
mosquito-example.science.2: A mosquito also carries something far smaller than itself: the malaria parasite is a single cell a few thousandths of a millimetre long.
mosquito-example.stats.0.label: Malaria deaths a year (WHO)
mosquito-example.stats.1.label: Ross finds malaria parasites in a mosquito
mosquito-example.stats.2.label: Nobel Prize for that discovery
mosquito-example.proof.0.title: Laveran: the parasite in the blood
mosquito-example.proof.0.text: Alphonse Laveran, an army doctor in Algeria, sees the malaria parasite in a patient's blood for the first time. Nobel Prize 1907.
mosquito-example.proof.1.title: Finlay: mosquitoes and yellow fever
mosquito-example.proof.1.text: Carlos Finlay proposes that mosquitoes carry yellow fever.
mosquito-example.proof.2.title: Ross: the parasite inside the mosquito
mosquito-example.proof.2.text: Ronald Ross finds the developing malaria parasite in the gut of an Anopheles mosquito that had fed on an infected patient. Nobel Prize 1902.

mosquito-example.proof.3.title: Reed: yellow fever proved
mosquito-example.proof.3.text: An American army commission under Walter Reed confirms, with human volunteers, that yellow fever is spread by mosquitoes.
mosquito-example.proof.4.title: The first malaria vaccine
mosquito-example.proof.4.text: The WHO recommends the first malaria vaccine, RTS,S, for children in areas of high risk.
mosquito-example.fit.0: The verse uses the mosquito as an example of something tiny that carries a large lesson; medicine has shown how much a mosquito can carry.
mosquito-example.fit.1: “Or what is above it” can be read as “what is smaller than it”, and the malaria parasite it carries is far smaller.
mosquito-example.gap.0: The verse does not mention disease; its point is that God uses humble examples.
mosquito-example.gap.1: Fawqahā is read both as “above it” (larger) and as “beyond it” (smaller).
mosquito-example.gap.2: People knew mosquitoes as pests long before science linked them to disease.

spider-house.title: The Spider's House
spider-house.hook: “The weakest of houses is the spider's house”: its silk is tougher than steel, but as a home it protects nothing.
spider-house.science.0: Spider silk is one of the toughest materials known. Weight for weight it rivals steel and beats Kevlar for toughness. In 2010 researchers measured the silk of Darwin's bark spider as the toughest biological material ever tested.
spider-house.science.1: But a web is a trap, not a shelter. It gives no protection from rain, wind, cold or enemies, and orb-weaving spiders often eat and respin theirs every day. As a house, it is truly frail.
spider-house.science.2: Biologists have also documented sexual cannibalism, where a female spider kills and eats her mate, in many species. Some modern writers read that into the verse's picture of a spider's household; classical commentators did not.
spider-house.stats.0.label: Silk of Darwin's bark spider measured as the toughest known
spider-house.stats.1.label: First spider-silk stockings and gloves (Bon)
spider-house.proof.0.title: Bon: clothes from spider silk
spider-house.proof.0.text: François Xavier Bon de Saint Hilaire makes stockings and gloves from spider silk and reports to the Royal Society of Montpellier.
spider-house.proof.1.title: McCook: spiders and their spinning
spider-house.proof.1.text: Henry McCook publishes American Spiders and Their Spinning-Work, a large study of how spiders build their webs.
spider-house.proof.2.title: Cannibalism in spiders
spider-house.proof.2.text: Mark Elgar and Bernard Crespi's book on cannibalism collects the evidence that in many species a female kills and eats her mate.
spider-house.proof.2.cap: A large female golden orb-weaver and her much smaller mate.
spider-house.proof.3.title: The toughest silk
spider-house.proof.3.text: Ingi Agnarsson and colleagues measure the silk of Darwin's bark spider, from Madagascar, as the toughest biological material ever tested.
spider-house.proof.3.cap: A female Argiope spider on her web.
spider-house.fit.0: As a shelter a web is very weak: it cannot keep out rain, wind, cold or enemies.
spider-house.fit.1: The verse's contrast, something that looks solid and gives no protection, matches silk that is tough while the web is fragile.
spider-house.gap.0: The verse is a moral parable about trusting anything other than God.
spider-house.gap.1: ʿAnkabūt is grammatically feminine, so the feminine verb does not by itself say the builder is female.
spider-house.gap.3: The verse says nothing about silk's strength or about mating; the cannibalism reading is modern and not found in classical commentary.

animal-communities.title: Communities Like You
animal-communities.hook: “No creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its wings, but is a community like you.” Zoologists have found societies in insects, birds and mammals.
animal-communities.science.0: Bees, ants and termites live in true societies with castes, division of labour and shared nests. E. O. Wilson's The Insect Societies (1971) laid out how they work.
animal-communities.science.1: Birds and mammals have societies too. In a starling murmuration each bird tracks about seven neighbours (2008). Vervet monkeys use different alarm calls for different predators (1980). Elephants call to each other in infrasound, too low for us to hear (1986). Bees tell each other where flowers are by dancing.
animal-communities.science.2: The picture that emerges is that even a tiny creature is part of a group with signals, roles and shared knowledge, which is close to what the verse says.

animal-communities.fit.0: Bees, ants and termites live in true societies with castes and division of labour: “communities like you”.
animal-communities.fit.1: Birds and mammals also live in flocks, herds and packs with signals and roles.
animal-communities.gap.0: Umam has also been read as “kinds” or “species”, each with its own nature.
animal-communities.gap.1: Many animals are solitary; the verse's point is that all creatures are God's creation and will be gathered to Him.
animal-communities.gap.2: It is not a statement about social behaviour as such.

camel-creation.title: Look at the Camels
camel-creation.hook: “Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?” Physiologists found a desert machine.
camel-creation.science.0: A camel's hump stores fat, not water, so it can go a long time without food. A thirsty camel can drink more than 100 litres in a few minutes, and can lose a quarter of its body weight in water and survive, which would kill most mammals.
camel-creation.science.1: In 1840 George Gulliver noticed that camels' red blood cells are oval, not round: they can swell with water without bursting. In 1956 Knut Schmidt-Nielsen showed that a camel lets its body temperature swing between about 34 and 41 °C, saving water it would have sweated away.
camel-creation.science.2: In 1993 researchers found that camels make antibodies built from a single chain, unlike ours. Fragments of them, called nanobodies, are now used in medicine; the first nanobody drug was approved in 2018.

camel-creation.fit.0: The verse asks people to look closely at camels; close study has found an animal remarkably built for the desert.
camel-creation.fit.1: It names the camel first, among the animals most familiar to the first audience.
camel-creation.gap.0: The verse gives no anatomy; it asks people to observe.
camel-creation.gap.1: The idea that the hump stores water is a myth; it stores fat.
camel-creation.gap.2: Arab herders knew the camel's endurance for centuries; the physiology is what science added.

bird-flight.title: Birds Spread and Fold Their Wings
bird-flight.hook: Birds “spread their wings and fold them”, and “none holds them but the Most Merciful.”
bird-flight.science.0: A bird flies by pushing air down and back with its wings, which are shaped so that the air pressure beneath is higher than above, producing lift. Birds alternate between wings spread wide to glide and soar, and wings folded in to reduce drag or to flap.
bird-flight.science.1: How lift works was understood only recently. Sir George Cayley separated lift from thrust around 1800. Otto Lilienthal made the first repeated glider flights in 1891. Martin Kutta and Nikolai Joukowski gave lift a mathematical theory around 1902–1906, and the Wright brothers flew a powered aeroplane in 1903.
bird-flight.science.2: Nothing visible holds a bird up: the air itself supports its weight, as long as the wing keeps moving through it.
bird-flight.stats.0.label: Lilienthal's first glider flights
bird-flight.stats.1.label: The Wright brothers' first powered flight
bird-flight.stats.2.label: Kutta–Joukowski theory of lift
bird-flight.proof.0.title: Cayley: lift and thrust
bird-flight.proof.0.text: Sir George Cayley separates the problem of flight into lift and thrust, and builds successful model gliders.
bird-flight.proof.1.title: Lilienthal: gliding by design
bird-flight.proof.1.text: Otto Lilienthal makes the first repeated, controlled glider flights, having studied the wings of storks for years.

bird-flight.proof.3.title: The Wright brothers
bird-flight.proof.3.text: Orville and Wilbur Wright fly the first powered, controlled aeroplane.
bird-flight.fit.0: Spreading and folding wings (ṣāffāt, yaqbiḍna) describe the two modes of bird flight: gliding and flapping.
bird-flight.fit.1: “None holds them” fits birds being carried by air alone, with no visible support.
bird-flight.gap.0: The verse points to God as the one who sustains; science explains the mechanism (lift), and the two readings can sit together.
bird-flight.gap.1: Anyone can watch birds spread and fold their wings, so the verse invites reflection rather than revealing hidden information.

three-darknesses.title: Three Darknesses
three-darknesses.hook: “He creates you in your mothers' wombs… within three darknesses”: the unborn child lies behind three layers.
three-darknesses.science.0: The developing child lies behind three layers: the front wall of the mother's abdomen, the wall of the uterus, and the amniotic sac with its two membranes (the amnion and the chorion). The layers keep light out, cushion the child, and help guard against infection.
three-darknesses.science.1: Inside, the amniotic fluid, about 800 millilitres at its peak around weeks 34 to 36, protects the child from knocks and keeps its temperature steady.
three-darknesses.science.2: Classical commentators named three darknesses too, though a slightly different three: the belly, the womb and the membrane around the child.
three-darknesses.stats.0.label: Layers: abdominal wall, uterine wall, amniotic membranes
three-darknesses.stats.1.label: Amniotic fluid at its peak (weeks 34–36)
three-darknesses.proof.0.title: Vesalius draws the pregnant uterus
three-darknesses.proof.0.text: Andreas Vesalius, in his great anatomy, shows the uterus opened to reveal the child inside its membranes.
three-darknesses.proof.1.title: William Hunter's atlas
three-darknesses.proof.1.text: William Hunter publishes The Anatomy of the Human Gravid Uterus, with life-size engravings of the child, its membranes and the wall of the uterus.
three-darknesses.proof.2.title: Ian Donald: ultrasound
three-darknesses.proof.2.text: Ian Donald and colleagues use ultrasound to look inside the womb for the first time; the layers around the child can now be seen in a living pregnancy.
three-darknesses.fit.0: Three layers surround the unborn child: the abdominal wall, the uterine wall and the amniotic membranes.
three-darknesses.fit.1: Each layer shuts out light, so the child develops in darkness.
three-darknesses.gap.0: Classical commentators listed the belly, the womb and the membrane around the child: a slightly different three.
three-darknesses.gap.1: “Darkness” may be figurative for concealment and protection.
three-darknesses.gap.2: The number three may be meant simply as “layers”.
